title: Notes With Built-In Practice and Answers
whatYouGet: Concept notes paired with graded practice and a clean answer key.
howToUse: Name the topic, paste the prompt, and hand out the study-plus-practice sheet.
effectiveUsage: 1. Type the topic and class.
2. Paste the prompt.
3. Check the practice difficulty fits.
4. Ask for more easy or hard items.
commonFix: If an answer looks off, reply: "Re-solve practice Q[n] step by step and verify the answer two different ways."
promptText:
ROLE: Act as a mathematics teacher who pairs clear notes with well-graded practice.

CONTEXT: I teach [CLASS/GRADE] for [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board / JEE / NEET]. I want a single handout on [TOPIC NAME] that teaches the concept and then lets students practise, with answers they can self-check. It should work as both a study sheet and a worksheet.

YOUR TASK:
1. Write concise concept notes (definitions, formulas, key methods) for the topic.
2. Give 2 fully worked model examples that mirror the practice to come.
3. Provide 10 practice questions graded easy (3), medium (4), hard (3).
4. Provide a clean answer key with one-line working for each answer, placed only at the very end.

INPUT: Here is the topic: [TOPIC NAME]. If I paste a difficulty target or sample question, match its style and level.

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Solve every model example and every practice question internally, then VERIFY each final answer by two independent checks before writing it. Never invent formulas or values. Keep all mathematics legible in clean LaTeX or clear plain text, one step per line in worked solutions.

OUTPUT FORMAT (in this order):
1. Title: [TOPIC NAME] - Notes and Practice
2. Concept Notes (definitions, formulas, methods)
3. Model Examples (Example 1, Example 2 - full steps)
4. Practice Questions (Easy 1-3, Medium 4-7, Hard 8-10, clearly labelled)
5. Answer Key (one-line working per answer, at the very end only)

RULES: Practice must truly match the difficulty labels. No answers shown beside questions. Everything standard and exam-correct. Verified answers only. State one assumption line if scope is unclear.

OUTPUT FILE FORMAT: present the complete result as a clean, ready-to-use document I can paste straight into Microsoft Word or Google Docs - a clear bold title, section headings, neatly numbered items, comfortable spacing, and simple tables only where helpful (avoid heavy formatting that breaks on paste). It must also print cleanly to PDF on A4 (File > Print > Save as PDF). Keep all mathematics fully readable (fractions as a/b, powers as x^2, roots as sqrt(x)).

MATHS FORMATTING: Write ALL mathematics so it reads correctly in a normal chat and pastes cleanly into Word or Google Docs. Use plain readable notation - for example a/b for fractions, x^2 for powers, sqrt(x) for roots, and symbols like <=, >=, !=, +-, pi, theta, integral and sum. Do NOT output raw LaTeX or code such as \frac{}{}, \sqrt{}, x^{2}, $...$ or \( ... \) - these appear as broken symbols to a teacher in a free chat.

CONTEXT CHECK: Before you begin, if any [SQUARE-BRACKET] above is still empty, or I have not given you the question / photo / data you need, ask me for exactly those and wait - never guess, and never answer with the placeholder text still in brackets.

GROUND RULES (always follow): Do not invent statistics, percentages, marks distributions you were not given, exam cut-offs, solve-time figures, NCERT or textbook page/line numbers, citations, or historical exam data. If you are unsure of any fact or number, say so and clearly label it an estimate; keep established fact separate from your own inference. Every step must be mathematically correct and at the stated class/board/exam level.

SIGNATURE: End your ENTIRE response with exactly this footer block (keep the lines and symbols):

title: Turn One Chapter Into a Complete Study System
whatYouGet: One pasted chapter or set of notes converted into a full study system - learning objectives, concept map, misconception list, graded question bank with answer key, and a spaced-review schedule - with every line traceable to what you pasted.
howToUse: Paste the chapter text or your class notes into the prompt, state the exam it is for and how far away it is, then send.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste real material into [SOURCE_MATERIAL] - a textbook chapter, your class notes, or a typed summary; the richer the paste, the better the system.
2. Name the exam in [TARGET_USE] (e.g. 'CBSE Class 10 boards' or 'JEE Main') so questions match the right difficulty.
3. Set [REVIEW_HORIZON] to the real time left, e.g. 'exam in 3 weeks', so the spaced schedule is usable.
4. Do the Question Bank with the Answer Key covered - it is built for active recall, not reading.
5. Check the 'Verify Externally' list: it names exactly what your notes were missing, so you know what to look up in the textbook.
commonFix: If the output includes facts or formulas that were not in your notes, reply: 'You added content not present in my source. Remove it or move it to Verify Externally, and re-tag every objective as STATED or IMPLIED.'
promptText:
ROLE
You are a learning-systems designer for mathematics who converts raw source material into a complete, active study system. Your iron rule: the system teaches what the source actually contains - you do not import outside formulas or results, and you mark every place where the source is thin so the student knows what to look up in the textbook.

INPUTS
- Source material: [SOURCE_MATERIAL] (paste the chapter, class notes, or summary here)
- Class / topic: [SUBJECT] (e.g. Class 11 - Sequences and Series)
- Preparing for: [TARGET_USE] (e.g. CBSE boards, ICSE, JEE Main, school unit test)
- Review horizon: [REVIEW_HORIZON] (e.g. exam in 3 weeks / ongoing retention)

PROCESS (internal; show only the output sections)
1. Read the source and extract only what it supports. Tag every claim you carry forward: STATED (explicit in source), IMPLIED (a fair mathematical consequence the source backs), or ABSENT (needed for [TARGET_USE] but missing).
2. Derive learning objectives from STATED + IMPLIED content, each phrased as an observable can-do ('Be able to...').
3. Build a concept map showing how the source's ideas connect (prerequisite, special case, contrast, derives-from), using only relationships the source establishes or clearly implies.
4. Write recall, application, and challenge questions that escalate in demand, each traceable to a location or idea in the source.
5. Design a spaced-review schedule fitted to [REVIEW_HORIZON].
6. List every ABSENT item honestly as a gap to check in the textbook - never silently fill it.

OUTPUT (exact sections)
## Coverage Snapshot
Three to five lines: what this source covers well, and what [TARGET_USE] needs that the source does NOT contain. If the source is too sparse for a full system, say so and scope down rather than inventing content.

## Learning Objectives
Numbered can-do statements, each tagged [STATED] or [IMPLIED].

## Concept Map
An indented or arrow-notation map of the key ideas and how they connect, with relationship types labeled.

## Definitions, Formulas & Key Methods
The essential terms, formulas and techniques, each in the source's own sense, one tight line each, with conditions of validity where the source gives them.

## Worked Example(s)
Only if the source provides or clearly supports one; reproduce it step by step. If none is supportable, write 'No worked example is grounded in this source' and move on.

## Misconception Watch
Likely wrong readings of this material, each with the correcting line from the source.

## Question Bank
Three labeled blocks - Recall / Application / Challenge - numbered questions, each with a (source: location or idea) tag. Match difficulty to [TARGET_USE].

## Answer Key
Concise worked answers keyed to question numbers, each grounded in the source.

## Spaced-Review Schedule
A dated or interval-based plan across [REVIEW_HORIZON]: what to review when, escalating from recognition to closed-book solving, with a final self-test checkpoint.

## Verify Externally
The gap list restated as concrete things to confirm from the textbook or teacher before the exam.

RULES
- Introduce no formula, theorem, or result not present in or fairly implied by [SOURCE_MATERIAL]. When tempted, route it to Verify Externally instead.
- Every question must be answerable from the source; if it is not, it belongs in the gap list, not the bank.
- No filler and no generic study tips untethered from this material.

YOUR TASK:
1. Read the topic I give you and pick ONE single idea that fits in 60 seconds.
2. Write a spoken-word script of about 120 to 140 words (roughly 55 to 60 seconds at a calm pace).
3. Open with a 3-second hook that creates curiosity or names a common mistake.
4. Deliver the one concept with exactly one clean worked example.
5. End with a one-line takeaway and a call-to-action (follow / save / comment).

INPUT: Here is the topic and level: [PASTE THE TOPIC AND CLASS LEVEL HERE].

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Solve the example fully in your head first. Then VERIFY the final answer by two independent methods (for example, substitute back, or re-do by a different rule). Never invent formulas or values; if a step needs a standard formula, state it correctly. Keep every piece of maths legible in clean plain text or simple LaTeX so it can be shown on screen.

SETUP (3-12s): the question or mistake, in plain speech.

PAYOFF (45-55s): the clean final answer and the one-line takeaway.
CTA (55-60s): the call-to-action line.

VERIFICATION NOTE: one line confirming the answer was checked two ways.

RULES: Total spoken words must be 120 to 140. Use short sentences a teacher can read aloud naturally. No jargon the student would not know. One concept only. Mathematically flawless.

title: Hook + Payoff Short That Keeps Viewers Watching
whatYouGet: A short script engineered around a curiosity gap that pays off at the end.
howToUse: Give a surprising math fact or result; the AI builds a tease-then-reveal short.
effectiveUsage: 1. Open any free AI chat.
2. Paste the prompt and your fact.
3. Pick your favourite hook option.
4. Record tease first, reveal last.
5. Ask for more hook variants if needed.
commonFix: If the hook is weak, reply: "Give me 5 bolder hook options that promise a surprise, and keep the reveal honest."
promptText:
ROLE: Act as a short-form retention specialist who writes maths shorts that hold attention to the last second.

CONTEXT: This is a 30 to 45 second vertical short for [CLASS/GRADE] students of [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board / JEE / NEET]. The whole video is built on a curiosity gap: a hook that promises something surprising, and a payoff that delivers it. The teacher speaks to camera.

YOUR TASK:
1. Take the maths fact, result, or trick I give you.
2. Write a hook that opens a curiosity gap in the first 3 seconds (give 3 hook options).
3. Build tension by hinting at the surprise without revealing it.
4. Deliver the payoff with one clean, correct demonstration.
5. Close with a one-line CTA.

INPUT: Here is the fact, result or trick: [PASTE IT HERE], for class level [CLASS/GRADE].

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Confirm the fact is actually true before writing. Solve or demonstrate it fully, then VERIFY by two independent checks. Never overstate or invent; the payoff must be genuinely correct. Keep the on-screen maths legible in plain text or LaTeX.

OUTPUT FORMAT (in this order):
HOOK OPTIONS: 3 spoken hook lines (pick-one).
TEASE (3-10s): spoken lines that build curiosity.
PAYOFF (10-35s): the spoken reveal with the worked demonstration; show on-screen maths in [BRACKETS].
FINAL ANSWER/RESULT: stated clearly.
CTA (35-45s): one line.
ON-SCREEN TEXT: 4 caption phrases.
VERIFICATION NOTE: how the result was checked two ways.

RULES: The payoff must honestly match the hook's promise. Total spoken words under 110. No clickbait that the maths cannot deliver. Flawless, legible maths.

FORMAT THE OUTPUT — PRIMARY DELIVERABLE:
Return one complete, editable document ready to paste into Word or Google Docs. Use a descriptive title, short section headings, readable paragraphs, numbered actions and tables only where they make the material easier to use. Include every requested section; do not return formatting advice instead of the document.


MATHS FORMATTING: Write ALL mathematics so it reads correctly in a normal chat and pastes cleanly into Word or Google Docs. Use plain readable notation - for example a/b for fractions, x^2 for powers, sqrt(x) for roots, and symbols like <=, >=, !=, +-, pi, theta, integral and sum. Do NOT output raw LaTeX or code such as \frac{}{}, \sqrt{}, x^{2}, $...$ or \( ... \) - these appear as broken symbols to a teacher in a free chat.
Footer: At the very end add a footer line: "Prepared by [YOUR NAME]", and put "Compiled by [YOUR NAME]" in the header block.

CONTEXT CHECK: Before you begin, if any [SQUARE-BRACKET] above is still empty, or I have not given you the question / photo / data you need, ask me for exactly those and wait - never guess, and never answer with the placeholder text still in brackets.

GROUND RULES (always follow): Do not invent statistics, percentages, marks distributions you were not given, exam cut-offs, solve-time figures, NCERT or textbook page/line numbers, citations, or historical exam data. If you are unsure of any fact or number, say so and clearly label it an estimate; keep established fact separate from your own inference. Every step must be mathematically correct and at the stated class/board/exam level.

SIGNATURE: End your ENTIRE response with exactly this footer block (keep the lines and symbols):
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔗 Free tools & to reach me: https://yosoyun.github.io/math-prompt-studio/
Questions, feedback or appreciation are always welcome.
